name: Buridan's Ass
statement: A donkey placed exactly between two identical piles of hay, with no reason to prefer either, would starve unable to choose.
meaning: Buridan's ass is a philosophical illustration about free will and rational choice. It imagines a hungry donkey placed exactly midway between two equally attractive, equidistant piles of hay, or in some versions between hay and water. Having no rational grounds to prefer one over the other, the ass cannot choose and starves to death. The paradox is named satirically after the fourteenth-century French philosopher Jean Buridan, who lived roughly from 1300 to 1361, though the donkey example is nowhere in his surviving writings; it was coined by critics to parody his account of moral choice. The scenario has ancient antecedents, including a passage in Aristotle's On the Heavens describing a man equally hungry and thirsty caught between food and drink, and a version in the medieval Persian thinker al-Ghazali. It sharpens the question of whether a purely rational will can ever choose between perfectly equal options.
mechanism: The puzzle presses on a view of the will as determined by reason and the greater good. If the will must always follow the stronger reason, then faced with two options judged perfectly equal, a strictly rational agent has no reason to move either way and is paralysed, so the donkey starves. Buridan himself defended a form of moral determinism, holding that the will chooses what the intellect judges best; confronted with equal alternatives he thought one should suspend judgment and defer choice until circumstances reveal a better option. Critics mocked this deferral with the starving ass, turning it into a reductio of his position. The scenario also engages the principle of sufficient reason, that nothing happens without a reason. Leibniz invoked this principle to dissolve the paradox, arguing that a perfectly symmetrical situation never actually arises, since minute, even unconscious, differences always tip the balance one way, so no real agent is ever truly poised between exactly equal options.

examples.text: The donkey stands exactly between two identical, equally tempting piles of hay; with no reason to choose either, it cannot decide and starves through indecision.
Aristotle's On the Heavens describes a man equally hungry and thirsty and equally placed between food and drink, an early version of the equal-options paralysis.
Leibniz argued by the principle of sufficient reason that perfect symmetry never really occurs, since tiny hidden differences always break the tie, so the ass would not starve.

variants.name: The liberty of indifference
variants.text: The idea that the will can make an arbitrary choice between equal options with no sufficient reason, which the paradox tests against rational determinism.

variants.name: The sufficient-reason dissolution
variants.text: Leibniz's response that the perfectly balanced case never arises, since minute differences always provide a reason that tips the decision.

whyItMatters: Buridan's ass is a classic, proverbial illustration in debates about free will, determinism, and rational choice, dramatizing the problem of how an agent can decide between perfectly equal options. It challenges any picture of the will as strictly bound to follow the greater reason, since such a will seems paralysed by a tie, and it thereby raises the question of whether genuine freedom requires the capacity to choose without a sufficient reason. The puzzle connects to Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason and to later discussions of decision-making, symmetry-breaking, and indifference. As a memorable image that turns an abstract problem about the will into a starving donkey, it has kept its place in philosophy and in ordinary speech as a byword for the paralysis of perfectly balanced indecision.

working.text: place the agent between two alternatives judged perfectly equal and equidistant, so no reason favours one over the other.
if the will must act only on the stronger reason, a perfect tie leaves it with no reason to move, and paralysis follows.
consider replies like Leibniz's, that exact symmetry never really occurs, or that the will has a liberty to choose arbitrarily between equals.

limits: Buridan's ass is a thought illustration about the will, not a claim that real donkeys starve between haystacks; its point is conceptual, and defenders of free choice reply that an agent can simply pick one option arbitrarily. Leibniz argued the perfectly symmetric case never actually arises, so the paradox may rest on an idealisation that never occurs in nature. The example is also misattributed: it is named after Jean Buridan satirically by his critics and is not found in his own works, so it caricatures rather than states his considered view. And it bears on a specific model of the will as purely reason-determined, leaving untouched accounts on which choice can proceed without a decisive reason. So it is a provocation about rational choice rather than a demonstrated result.
misreadings: The example is not actually Buridan's own; it was coined by critics to parody his view, so attributing the starving-donkey story to his writings is mistaken. The point is not that indecision is common but that a will bound strictly to the greater reason seems unable to choose between exact equals, a challenge to one theory of the will. And the paradox is not left standing unanswered: Leibniz and others argue that perfect symmetry never truly occurs, or that the will can choose arbitrarily, so treating the ass as proof that rational agents must be paralysed overstates the case.
origin: Named satirically after the fourteenth-century French philosopher Jean Buridan by his critics, though the donkey example is absent from his own works; it parodies his moral determinism, and has antecedents in Aristotle's On the Heavens and in al-Ghazali.
